text: Matthew Langford Perry (August 19, 1969 – October 28, 2023) was an American and Canadian actor known internationally for his role as Chandler Bing on the NBC sitcom Friends (1994–2004). He also appeared in Ally McBeal (2002), received Primetime Emmy Award nominations for his performances in The West Wing (2003) and The Ron Clark Story (2006), and played leading roles in films including Fools Rush In (1997), Almost Heroes (1998), Three to Tango (1999), The Whole Nine Yards (2000), Serving Sara (2002), The Whole Ten Yards (2004), and 17 Again (2009). Perry was the co-creator, co-writer, executive producer, and star of the ABC sitcom Mr. Sunshine, which aired from February to April 2011. In August 2012, he starred as sportscaster Ryan King on the NBC sitcom Go On. He co-developed and starred in a revival of the CBS sitcom The Odd Couple from 2015 to 2017, portraying Oscar Madison. He had recurring roles in The Good Wife (2012–2013) and The Good Fight (2017), portrayed Ted Kennedy in The Kennedys: After Camelot (2017), and appeared as himself in Friends: The Reunion (2021). He voiced Benny in the video game Fallout: New Vegas (2010). Born in Williamstown, Massachusetts, on August 19, 1969, Perry's mother, Suzanne Marie Morrison (née Langford, born 1948), is a Canadian journalist who served as press secretary to Canadian prime minister Pierre Trudeau; his father, John Bennett Perry (born 1941), is an American actor and former model. Perry's parents separated when he was one year old, and his mother married Canadian broadcast journalist Keith Morrison. He was mostly raised in Ottawa, Ontario, with brief stays in Toronto and Montreal, attending Rockcliffe Park Public School and Ashbury College. He had four younger maternal half-siblings—Caitlin, Emily, Will, and Madeline—and a younger paternal half-sister, Maria. By age 10, Perry began misbehaving, stealing money, smoking, letting his grades slip, and beating up future Canadian prime minister Justin Trudeau. He attributed his behavior to feeling like an outsider after his mother began having children with Morrison, writing, "I was so often on the outside looking in, still that kid up in the clouds on a flight to somewhere else, unaccompanied." At age 14, he began consuming alcohol and was drinking daily by his 18th birthday. He practiced tennis for up to 10 hours per day and became a top-ranked junior player in Canada, though his prospects declined after moving to Los Angeles at age 15 to live with his father. At 15, he began studying acting at the Buckley School in Sherman Oaks, graduating in 1987, and took improvisational comedy classes at L.A. Connection. His first credited role was in 240-Robert (1979) as a child actor. He made guest appearances on Not Necessarily the News (1983), Charles in Charge (1985), and Silver Spoons (1986), and played Chazz Russell in Second Chance (1987–1988). He made his film debut in A Night in the Life of Jimmy Reardon (1988) and had a three-episode arc on Growing Pains (1989) as Carol Seaver's boyfriend Sandy, who dies in a drunk driving incident. He was cast as a regular on the 1990 CBS sitcom Sydney, playing the younger brother of Valerie Bertinelli's character, and starred in the ABC sitcom Home Free (1993). His commitment to a pilot for LAX 2194, set in a futuristic Los Angeles airport, initially made him unavailable for a role in Six of One, later titled Friends. After the LAX 2194 pilot failed, he was cast as Chandler Bing in Friends at age 24, the youngest member of the main cast. While waiting for Friends to air, he performed at the Williamstown Theater Festival in 1993 alongside Gwyneth Paltrow. Friends became a massive success, making Perry an international celebrity; by 2002, he and his co-stars earned $1 million per episode, and he received an Emmy nomination in 2002 for Outstanding Lead Actor in a Comedy Series. In 1995, he and Jennifer Aniston appeared in a 60-minute promotional video for Microsoft's Windows 95. Perry received two Emmy nominations for Outstanding Guest Actor in a Drama Series for his role as Joe Quincy in The West Wing (2003 and 2004) and appeared in two episodes of Ally McBeal as attorney Todd Merrick. In 2004, he made his directorial debut in an episode of Scrubs, which included his father. He starred in the TNT movie The Ron Clark Story (premiered August 13, 2006), earning a Golden Globe and Emmy nomination. From 2006 to 2007, he appeared in Studio 60 on the Sunset Strip as Matt Albie alongside Bradley Whitford's Danny Tripp. In 2006, he began filming Numb, a film based on depersonalization disorder, which was released on DVD on May 13, 2008. He also appeared in David Mamet's Sexual Perversity in Chicago on stage in London and starred in the independent film Birds of America (2008). Showtime passed on a pilot called The End of Steve, a dark comedy written, produced, and starred in by Perry and Peter Tolan. In 2009, he starred in 17 Again, where a 37-year-old man transforms into his 17-year-old self (Zac Efron) after an accident; the film received mixed reviews but was a box-office success. A review on WRC-TV found Perry miscast, noting disbelief in Efron growing up to resemble Perry physically and behaviorally. In 2009, Perry presented Ellen DeGeneres with an Xbox 360 console and a copy of Fallout 3 on The Ellen DeGeneres Show, leading Obsidian Entertainment to cast him as the voice of Benny in Fallout: New Vegas (2010). His comedy pilot Mr. Sunshine, based on his original idea, was bought by ABC; he played a middle-aged man with an identity crisis, but the series was canceled after nine episodes in 2011. In 2012, he starred in Go On as Ryan King, a sportscaster trying to move on after his wife's death through mandatory therapy. He guest-starred as attorney Mike Kresteva on The Good Wife (2012–2013) and reprised the role in The Good Fight (2017). In 2014, he made his British television debut in The Dog Thrower, portraying a charismatic man who enchanted onlookers by throwing his dog in the air. From 2015 to 2017, he starred, co-wrote, and served as executive producer of the CBS reboot of The Odd Couple, playing Oscar Madison opposite Thomas Lennon as Felix Unger. He played the lead in the world premiere of his play The End of Longing, which opened on February 11, 2016, at the Playhouse Theatre in London, with a successful limited run despite mixed reviews. He restructured the play and appeared with Jennifer Morrison in its second off-Broadway production at the Lucille Lortel Theatre, opening on June 5, 2017, and closing on July 1 after poor reviews. Perry described the play as "a personal message to the world, an exaggerated form of me as a drunk. I had something important to say to people like me, and to people who love people like me." In March 2017, he reprised his role as Mike Kresteva in The Good Fight. Later that year, he starred as Ted Kennedy in The Kennedys: After Camelot. In May 2021, he participated in Friends: The Reunion. He was meant to have a role in Don't Look Up but withdrew in 2020 due to CPR-induced broken ribs. In October 2022, he released his memoir, Friends, Lovers, and the Big Terrible Thing, which became a bestseller on Amazon and The New York Times charts. Perry held American citizenship by birth and Canadian citizenship through his mother. He dated Yasmine Bleeth (1995), Julia Roberts (1995–1996), and Lizzy Caplan (2006–2012); in November 2020, he became engaged to literary manager Molly Hurwitz, ending the engagement in 2021. Residences owned by Perry included a condo in Sierra Towers purchased from Elton John, a house in Hollywood Hills, a house in Malibu, a cottage in Pacific Palisades, and a condo at the top floor of The Century in Los Angeles, purchased in 2017 for $20 million and sold in 2021 for $21.6 million. In June 2023, he purchased a mid-century modern house in Hollywood Hills. Perry had a perfectionist and obsessive personality, spending many hours perfecting his answering machine message and believed in God, describing himself as a "seeker" with a close relationship. In his memoir, he wrote that by age 14 he had become an alcoholic, became addicted to Vicodin after a jet ski accident in 1997, completed a 28-day rehab program at Hazelden Betty Ford Foundation that year, and took up to 55 Vicodin pills per day, dropping his weight to 128 pounds (58 kg). In May 2000, he was admitted to Cedars-Sinai Medical Center with alcohol-induced pancreatitis. In 2002, he said he tried not to drink on Friends but arrived with extreme hangovers and sometimes shook or sweated excessively; during later seasons, he was frequently drunk or high on set, and his castmates staged an intervention without success. In February 2001, he paused Friends and Serving Sara productions for two months to enter in-patient rehabilitation for Vicodin, methadone, amphetamines, and alcohol, and later stated he had no memory of three years of work on Friends. In 2018, he spent five months in the hospital for a gastrointestinal perforation, nearly dying from a colon burst due to opioid abuse, spending two weeks in a coma and using a colostomy bag for nine months; doctors gave him a 2% survival chance upon admission and he was connected to an ECMO machine. He faked pain to obtain 1,800 milligrams of hydrocodone per day and received daily ketamine infusions; during a surgery, he was given propofol that stopped his heart for five minutes, resulting in CPR and eight broken ribs. He paid $175,000 for a private jet to get drugs in Los Angeles, and when refused, booked another $175,000 flight to Switzerland. In 2022, he estimated spending $9 million on addiction, including 14 stomach surgeries, 15 rehab stays, therapy twice a week for 30 years, and attending approximately 6,000 Alcoholics Anonymous meetings. In July 2011, he lobbied U.S. Congress as a spokesperson for the National Association of Drug Court Professionals in support of drug court funding. In May 2013, he received the Champion of Recovery Award from the White House Office of National Drug Control Policy for opening Perry House, a rehab center in his former Malibu mansion. In 2015, he sold the mansion and relocated its services. During the COVID-19 pandemic, he launched an apparel line inspired by Friends, with proceeds donated to the World Health Organization's COVID-19 relief fund. On October 28, 2023, Perry was found unresponsive in a hot tub at his home in Pacific Palisades, Los Angeles, and was pronounced dead at 4:17 p.m. the same day at age 54. He died from accidental drowning caused by the acute effects of ketamine use. Five people were charged in connection with helping him acquire lethal doses of ketamine; all five pleaded guilty. Salvador Plasencia, a former California physician who supplied Perry with ketamine, was sentenced to 30 months in prison on December 3, 2025, and is currently in custody; Mark Chavez, another former California physician involved in ketamine distribution to Perry, was sentenced on December 16, 2025, to eight months of house arrest; Jasveen Sangha, who also pleaded guilty, is believed to have supplied the ketamine that caused his death. Perry's funeral was held on November 3, 2023, at Forest Lawn Memorial Park in Los Angeles, where he was buried. His father, mother, and stepfather attended, as did his five Friends co-stars. The Peter Gabriel and Kate Bush song "Don't Give Up" was played at the funeral, as Perry was enamored with the song and referenced it in signed copies of his autobiography to help people suffering from depression or addiction. Following his death, the National Philanthropic Trust established the Matthew Perry Foundation to support people suffering from addiction. On December 15, 2023, Perry's death was reported.

Matthew Perry, best known for his portrayal of Chandler Bing on Friends from 1994 to 2004, became one of television's most recognizable comic performers, with critics noting his precise timing and distinctive “could I be any more…?” cadence, which was widely imitated, as well as the vulnerability he brought to the character. Beyond acting, Perry advocated for addiction recovery; in 2013, he met with the White House Office of National Drug Control Policy to support drug courts and opened Perry House, a men's sober-living facility in his former Malibu home, which operated from 2013 to 2015. He expressed a desire to be remembered for helping people achieve sobriety rather than his acting career, a mission continued by the Matthew Perry Foundation, established after his death on November 3, 2023. During the COVID-19 pandemic, Perry launched an apparel line inspired by Friends, with all proceeds donated to the World Health Organization's COVID-19 relief fund. On October 28, 2023, Perry was found unresponsive in a hot tub at his home in Pacific Palisades, Los Angeles, and was pronounced dead at 4:17 p.m. the same day; he was 54 years old. The Los Angeles County Department of Medical Examiner determined that his death was due to acute effects of ketamine, with contributing factors including buprenorphine, drowning, and coronary artery disease. The report stated that at the high levels of ketamine found in his blood, the primary lethal effects were cardiovascular overstimulation and respiratory depression, with drowning occurring due to submersion after he lapsed into unconsciousness and coronary artery disease exacerbating ketamine’s effects on the heart. Perry had been receiving ketamine-assisted psychotherapy to treat anxiety, with his last session occurring the week before his death; however, the ketamine in his system at death could not have come from that session, as ketamine has a half-life of 3 to 4 hours or less. On December 15, 2023, the cause of death was revealed. In May 2024, the Los Angeles Police Department opened an investigation into how Perry obtained the high dose of ketamine that led to his death. On August 15, 2024, five individuals were indicted: Perry’s personal assistant, two doctors, and two drug dealers, including TV director Erik Fleming, for involvement in the distribution of ketamine that caused Perry’s death and that of another person. Three of the accused agreed to plead guilty; Kenneth Iwamasa and Erik Fleming entered guilty pleas shortly after being charged—on August 7 and August 8, 2024, respectively. Former doctor Mark Chavez, who had signed a plea agreement, had his guilty plea accepted during a court hearing on August 30, 2024, though he officially entered it on October 2, 2024. Salvador Plasencia, the second doctor, agreed to plead guilty on June 17, 2025, in court to four counts of ketamine distribution, after initially being scheduled for trial in August 2025. U.S. Attorney Martin Estrada stated that Perry paid the two doctors $55,000 in cash in the two months before his death. Iwamasa admitted to obtaining ketamine for Perry and injecting him with it, while Fleming admitted to obtaining ketamine from supplier Jasveen Sangha and giving it to Iwamasa for Perry to use. Text messages revealed that Plasencia purchased ketamine from Chavez, with one message showing Plasencia asking Chavez, "I wonder how much this moron will pay." Sangha, known as the "Ketamine Queen," was identified as the main supplier of the ketamine Perry used at the time of his death; her North Hollywood home, raided by U.S. DEA authorities in March 2024, was described as a "drug-selling emporium." Fleming admitted to obtaining 71 vials of ketamine from Sangha for Perry. Plasencia and Sangha were considered the primary targets in the case. On August 18, 2025, Sangha officially filed her guilty plea in court, admitting to one count of maintaining a drug-involved premises, three counts of ketamine distribution, and one count of distribution resulting in death or serious bodily injury. She had been in federal custody since her arrest in August 2024 and officially pleaded guilty to all five counts on September 3, 2025, before the U.S. District Court for the Central District of California. Sangha faces up to 45 years in prison. Plasencia, who remained free on bond until sentencing, faces up to 10 years per charge, totaling 40 years; Fleming, who pleaded guilty to one count of conspiracy to distribute ketamine and one count of distribution resulting in death, faces up to 25 years; Iwamasa, who pleaded guilty to one count of conspiracy to distribute ketamine causing death, faces up to 15 years; and Chavez, who pleaded guilty to one count of conspiracy to distribute ketamine, faces up to 10 years. Chavez had his medical license suspended, later confirmed as permanently given up, and Plasencia surrendered his California medical license in September 2025. Plasencia was sentenced on December 3, 2025, to 30 months in prison, two years of supervised release, and a $5,600 fine, and was taken into federal custody after sentencing. Chavez was sentenced on December 16, 2025, to eight months of house arrest, three years of supervised release, and 300 hours of community service. Fleming was scheduled for sentencing on January 7, 2026, and Iwamasa on January 14, 2026. The U.S. Attorney’s office confirmed that Sangha will be sentenced on February 25, 2026. Tributes to Perry reflected his impact: the main Friends cast issued a joint statement, Max added an on-screen memorial card to the series, and on August 19, 2025, co-star Salma Hayek marked what would have been Perry’s 56th birthday with an Instagram tribute.
